content: Deltamethrin, marketed as K-Othrine 250 WDG, is applied at a target dose of 25 mg of active ingredient per square meter. Pirimiphos-methyl, an organophosphate insecticide sold as Actellic 300 CS, is used at a target dose of 1 g of active ingredient per square meter. Bendiocarb, a carbamate insecticide branded as Ficam 80 WP, is applied at a target dose of 400 mg of active ingredient per square meter. In the case of extending recommendations to broflanilide, a detailed entomological comparison was conducted between Vectron™ T500, applied at a target dose of 100 mg of active ingredient per square meter, and pirimiphos-methyl (Actellic 300 CS). The data from these comparisons were reviewed by WHO technical expert groups, which subsequently advised the WHO on extending the IRS (indoor residual spraying) recommendations based on their findings. This advice was further evaluated by WHO’s Malaria Policy Advisory Group and, in the case of broflanilide, by the relevant Guideline Development Group (GDG) and the Guideline Review Committee (GRC) secretariat. As comparative efficacy assessments are now integrated into the evaluation process for malaria vector control, any future extensions of WHO recommendations for vector control will require, at a minimum, comparative effectiveness data. As of September 2023, no prequalified organochlorine IRS formulations, including DDT, are available. Consequently, no DDT product has been assessed by WHO for efficacy, safety, or quality in vector control, nor have manufacturing sites for DDT been inspected. Unlike other insecticide classes recommended by WHO for IRS, DDT is classified as a persistent organic pollutant. Its production and use are strictly regulated under the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, an international agreement established in 2004 to protect human health and the environment. The Convention allows an exemption for DDT use in disease vector control due to the lack of equally effective alternatives at the time. However, the recent expansion of IRS products and vector control interventions has provided additional options. WHO actively supports reducing and eventually eliminating DDT use while minimizing the burden of vector-borne diseases. DDT use for malaria vector control has declined over the years, and WHO encourages this trend. In certain areas, DDT use may still be justified, but decisions must be based on a detailed analysis of all available options, with clear reasoning for choosing DDT over alternatives. WHO considers DDT a last resort, not a first choice, and its use must comply with the conditions set by the Stockholm Convention. Strict control measures and adherence to national guidelines and WHO technical guidance are required for its use. Countries using DDT for malaria vector control must reassess its necessity at least every two years and report findings to the WHO Global Malaria Programme and the Stockholm Convention Secretariat. When selecting insecticides for IRS, it is crucial to evaluate the resistance profile of local vectors to ensure susceptibility. Continuous use of the same product in the same area over multiple seasons is discouraged, as it may lead to resistance in mosquitoes. Proactive planning for switching to alternative insecticides is recommended. Residual efficacy must also be considered, ensuring the insecticide remains effective throughout the transmission season and on various surfaces such as cement, mud, or wood. Community acceptance of IRS is critical for program success, as it requires householders to permit spray teams to enter their homes and remove personal items before spraying. Some formulations may leave unsightly residues or discolor painted surfaces, which can reduce acceptance. Repeated spraying over extended periods may lead to household refusal, hindering effective implementation. Information, education, and communication strategies are essential to maintain community support and cooperation. Reactive IRS, a focused approach targeting likely infection sites of index cases and their neighbors, is also an option. Monitoring the quality of insecticide application and residual activity through wall cone bioassays is essential. Entomological surveillance and environmental impact assessments should evaluate IRS effectiveness. Detailed guidance is available in the WHO publication Indoor Residual Spraying: An Operational Manual for Malaria Transmission, Control, and Elimination. A systematic review investigated the impact of residual surface treatment (RST) of insecticides on malaria compared to no vector control intervention. Only IRS studies met the inclusion criteria, with ten studies from Africa and Asia included. These studies provided very low-certainty evidence that all-age malaria parasite prevalence was lower in IRS areas than in non-IRS areas. However, due to variability in post-IRS measurement periods, a summary estimate of relative risk could not be calculated. Subgroup analyses on insecticide class and transmission intensity showed no significant modifying effects, and data on IRS coverage levels or insecticide resistance effects were insufficient for analysis. Adverse events associated with IRS were generally mild. In Pakistan, transient skin irritation and headaches were reported among spray personnel and participants, resolving within hours. Similar effects were observed in Tanzania, where spray personnel experienced facial paresthesia despite wearing protective equipment. The GDG judged the extent of undesirable effects to be small compared to no IRS. The systematic review did not identify research on preferences and values related to IRS. However, the GDG noted that IRS could increase equity by reducing mosquito populations community-wide, benefiting even those not directly receiving IRS. To enhance health equity, targeting populations most at risk for malaria is essential. Challenges such as wall discoloration, bad odors, increased bed bug nuisance, and food grain contamination were reported in India after DDT spraying. These factors may depend on the insecticide formulation and application method.
